notes.meaning: Paul tells the church to welcome a believer whose faith is "weak." He means someone with tender, overly strict scruples, not someone lacking saving faith. Welcome him warmly into fellowship, the way you would offer him your hand. Don't invite him in just to argue him out of his doubts, because harsh debate usually makes the doubts stronger.

One believer is sure he may eat any food. Another eats only vegetables. Many writers think this second person still felt bound by the old Jewish food laws. Others think he feared buying meat that had been offered to idols. Either way, he avoided meat altogether to be safe.

Each side had its own typical fault. The free eater looked down on the careful one as fussy. The careful one condemned the free eater as careless about God's law. Paul corrects both, because God has welcomed this person as His child. If God has accepted someone, we dare not reject them.

It is rude to scold someone else's servant, and every believer is Christ's servant, not ours. Whether he is approved or not is up to his own Master. Paul adds a hopeful word: he will stand, because the Lord is able to hold him up. So we should lean toward hoping well of a fellow believer.

A second example is special days. Believers from a Jewish background still honored feasts like Passover and the new moons. Others treated every day as the Lord's. Paul does not settle it by command. Each person should be fully convinced in his own mind and act by a settled conscience.

differ.view: Paul means only the Jewish feast days. The weekly Lord's Day, which all early Christians kept, is not in view and remains a holy day.
Whether and on which day a Christian keeps a Sabbath rest is a matter of conscience, and no one should judge another over it.
Special days have no absolute command behind them, but they are spiritually useful, which is good reason to keep the church's calendar.

notes.meaning: Both people are trying to honor the Lord. The one who keeps the day does it for God. The one who eats freely thanks God for his food, and the one who holds back thanks God for his vegetables. A thankful heart toward God makes either meal holy, and this shows Christians said grace at meals.

No Christian is his own master or lives just to please himself. Our whole life, and even our death, belongs to the Lord Jesus. This is one thing strong and weak believers share, however much they differ in small matters. Since we all belong to Him, we have no right to act as each other's masters.

Christ died and rose again so that He would be Lord over everyone, the living and the dead. He paid for this right with His own life. So we must not grab His place by sitting in judgment on our brothers' consciences.

Paul speaks to both sides in turn. To the strict believer he says: why do you judge your brother? To the free believer he says: why do you look down on him? We will all stand together before God's judgment seat, so it is absurd for one person on trial to climb up into the judge's chair.

Paul quotes Isaiah 45:23, where God makes a solemn promise by His own life. One day every knee will bow and every tongue will confess Him. Paul applies these words about the Lord God to Christ the Judge, which shows that Jesus is truly God.

Each of us will answer to God for himself, not for anyone else. Others are not answerable to us, and we are not answerable for them. That leaves plenty of work searching our own hearts. Someone who judges himself strictly will be slow to judge his brother.

Paul plays on the word "judge." Stop judging each other, and instead make this your judgment: never trip up a brother. A "stumbling block" is anything that leads another believer into sin, upsets him, or hinders his walk with God.

Paul is sure, through the Lord Jesus, that no food is unclean in itself. The old food laws ended with Christ. Still, if someone believes a food is wrong, it is wrong for him, because eating it would mean going against his conscience. A mistaken conscience can make a good thing wrong for that person, but it can never make an evil thing good.

Paul now speaks to the strong. If your eating upsets your brother, you are no longer walking in love. Christ gave His life for that brother, so surely you can give up a meal for him. Pushing him to act against his conscience, or to turn from the faith, puts his soul in real danger.

differ.view: This verse shows that a person for whom Christ died can actually be lost.
True believers will be kept by God to the end. The warning shows how serious our conduct is, and it is one of the means God uses to keep His people.

notes.meaning: "Your good" is your Christian freedom, and in the end the gospel itself. Don't use that freedom so carelessly that people call it reckless and speak badly of it. We can't stop every critic, but we shouldn't give them a reason.

God's kingdom, meaning His rule in our lives, is not about what we eat or drink. It is about righteousness: being right with God through Christ and living rightly. It is about peace with one another. And it is about the joy the Holy Spirit gives in our hearts. These are the things that really matter.
Whoever serves Christ by living this way pleases God. Wise and good people will also respect such a life, even if some critics never do.

So we should go after whatever brings peace and helps others grow. To "edify" means to build up, like building a house. Christians agree on far more than they differ on, so we should put our energy there.
Don't tear down God's work over food. That work is the faith and grace God is building in your brother's life. All food is clean, but eating becomes wrong when it trips up another believer.

It is better to give up meat, wine, or anything else than to make a brother stumble. These things are allowed, but we don't need them, and love gladly sets them aside. Paul is talking about protecting a weaker believer's sincere conscience. He is not giving in to people who demand rules, and this is not a lifelong ban.

"Faith" here means your settled belief about such matters, not saving faith. Keep it between you and God, and don't flaunt it where it could hurt others. Happy is the person whose conscience does not accuse him for what he chooses to do.

If someone doubts and eats anyway, his own conscience condemns him, because he did not act from faith. "Faith" here means a firm conviction that God approves. Anything done while doubting it is right becomes sin for that person. So when in doubt, take the safe path.

differ.view: The verse reaches wider: sin is anything not rooted in trusting God, so everything an unbeliever does falls short.
